segments.text:
Verſ. 29.
Shall I not viſit vpon this, ſaith the Lord? And ſhall not my ſoule be auenged vpon ſuch a nation as this?

HE yet repeats that which we ſaw before: and ſo this verſe ſhall need no long expoſition. But this repetition is no way ſuperfluous. For the Iewes were ſo hardened, that they ſcorned all reprehenſions and threatnings. This is the cauſe why God heere riſeth vp with greater vehemency of ſpeech, and ſaith, ſhall I not viſit vpon theſe things? He takes this for a reſolued truth, whereof we alſo ought to be well perſwaded; namely, that God is the Iudge of all the world. Now it is the proper office of a Iudge, to puniſh malefactors; alſo to ſuccour the poore that are vnworthily oppreſſed, and to repreſſe the pride of ſuch as giue themſelues leaue to doe euill. God then vſeth an argument heere, taken from his nature and office: as if he ſhould ſay, Can I that am God, ſuffer this ſo hatefull an impiety, this pride and preſumption of my people, to haue the ſwing on this manner, without executing my vengeance on them.

And ſhall not my ſoule be auenged on ſuch a nation as this? Heere (as wee haue ſaid elſewhere) God attributes that to his perſon, which properly appertaines not vnto him. But it is all one as if hee had ſaid, Among earthly Iudges,
none are found ſo remiſſe, that can put vp ſuch indignities, and outrages. For when a Iudge ſhall perceiue the people ſcorne him, will he (thinke you) take it well at their hands? Shall not my ſoule then be auenged? As if hee ſhould ſay, I am not ſo ſlothfull nor careleſſe, but in the end, be ſure I will pay you home, for this contempt, ſo full of pride and ouerweening. It followes.
